heroes.name: Gobekli Tepe
heroes.summary: Monumental enclosures of carved T-shaped pillars raised by pre-agricultural people, buried deliberately and excavated from 1995. The oldest known monumental architecture.
heroes.debated: How a society without farming organised the labour, and why the enclosures were periodically buried.

heroes.name: Stonehenge
heroes.summary: A ring of sarsen and bluestone uprights on Salisbury Plain, raised in stages from about 3000 BCE. Excavation has traced its earthwork ditch, timber predecessors and long distance stone transport.
heroes.debated: How the bluestones reached the site from Wales, and whether the monument was primarily a calendar, a cemetery or a gathering place.

heroes.name: Avebury
heroes.summary: The largest stone circle in Britain, enclosing a village within a huge henge bank and ditch, built in phases from about 2850 BCE. Avenues of paired stones link it to nearby monuments.
heroes.debated: The order in which the henge, circles and avenues were built, and what ceremonies the enclosed space was used for.

heroes.name: Newgrange
heroes.summary: A grass covered passage tomb in the Boyne Valley, older than Stonehenge and the Giza pyramids. Its roof box aligns with sunrise at the winter solstice, lighting the inner chamber.
heroes.debated: Whether the mound served mainly as a tomb, an astronomical marker or both, and how its quartz facade originally looked.

heroes.name: Callanish
heroes.summary: A cruciform arrangement of gneiss standing stones on the Isle of Lewis, raised around 2900 BCE and used for some 1,500 years before peat gradually buried its base.
heroes.debated: The circle's original purpose, and how its avenue and lunar alignments were meant to be read.

heroes.name: Alignements de Menec
heroes.summary: Thousands of standing stones in Brittany run in long parallel rows, with the Menec alignment among the largest. Erected over centuries from about 4500 BCE by Neolithic farming communities.
heroes.debated: Why the rows were laid out as they are, and whether they tracked astronomical, ritual or territorial purposes.

heroes.name: Ggantija
heroes.summary: Twin megalithic temples on Gozo, among the oldest free standing stone structures known, built from about 3600 BCE using massive coralline limestone blocks.
heroes.debated: How Neolithic builders without metal tools or draught animals moved and raised such large blocks.

heroes.name: Baalbek trilithon
heroes.summary: A Roman temple complex raised over an older Phoenician sanctuary, its podium built from some of the largest cut stones ever quarried, including the unfinished Stone of the Pregnant Woman.
heroes.debated: How the trilithon's blocks, each roughly 800 tonnes, were quarried, moved and set, and how much of the platform predates Roman building.

heroes.name: Nabta Playa
heroes.summary: A small stone circle and alignments in the Nubian desert, raised by cattle herding Neolithic communities around a seasonal lake. Among the earliest known structures with astronomical alignments.
heroes.debated: Which stars or solar events the alignments were meant to track, and how precise the intended astronomy really was.
heroes.attribution: Academic survey: Malville, 'Astronomy of Nabta Playa'

heroes.name: Great Zimbabwe
heroes.summary: Dry stone enclosures and a conical tower mark the capital of a Shona trading state, built from about 1100 CE and abandoned by the 15th century after its wealth peaked on the gold and ivory trade.
heroes.debated: How large the resident population was at its height, and the extent of its trade links with the Swahili coast.

heroes.name: Derinkuyu
heroes.summary: An underground city cut into Cappadocia's soft volcanic rock, with ventilation shafts, wells and stables across many levels. Used for shelter and storage over successive periods into Byzantine times.
heroes.debated: Who first excavated the earliest levels, and how large a population it could shelter at once.

heroes.name: Mohenjo-daro
heroes.summary: A planned Bronze Age city of the Indus Valley civilisation, with grid streets, standardised baked brick and an advanced drainage system, excavated from the 1920s.
heroes.debated: Why the city was abandoned by around 1900 BCE, and how its still undeciphered script should be read.

heroes.name: Plain of Jars, site 1
heroes.summary: Thousands of carved stone jars scattered across Xiangkhouang, the largest cluster at site 1, linked to Iron Age funerary practice. Unexploded ordnance still restricts access to many fields.
heroes.debated: The jars' exact purpose, whether primary burial, secondary burial or storage, and who quarried and moved them.

heroes.name: Nazca lines
heroes.summary: Hundreds of geoglyphs scored into the Peruvian desert floor by the Nazca culture, depicting animals, plants and geometric lines, some running for kilometres and best seen from the air.
heroes.debated: Why the lines were made, whether for ritual walking paths, water related ceremony or astronomical marking.

heroes.name: Sacsayhuaman
heroes.summary: A massive Inca stone complex above Cusco, its zigzag walls built from close fitted limestone blocks weighing many tonnes, part of a wider defensive and ceremonial precinct.
heroes.debated: Whether its primary role was military defence, religious ceremony or both, and how the blocks were shaped and fitted so precisely.
heroes.attribution: UNESCO World Heritage listing (City of Cuzco)

heroes.name: Puma Punku
heroes.summary: A ceremonial platform at Tiwanaku on the Andean altiplano, known for precisely cut andesite and sandstone blocks that once formed a larger terraced structure, now largely collapsed.
heroes.debated: How the stones were cut and finished with such precision, and how large the original superstructure was.

heroes.name: Serpent Mound
heroes.summary: A quarter mile effigy mound in Ohio shaped like an uncoiling serpent, built on a ridge above a creek. Radiocarbon dates have suggested more than one construction episode.
heroes.debated: Which culture built it and when, with radiocarbon results pointing to both an early Adena date and a later Fort Ancient date.

heroes.name: Poverty Point
heroes.summary: Concentric earthen ridges and mounds raised by hunter gatherers in the Mississippi Valley, built without agriculture or pottery, among the largest earthworks of their age in the Americas.
heroes.debated: How a non-agricultural society organised the labour to move so much earth, and what the ridges were used for.

heroes.name: Yonaguni monument
heroes.summary: A submerged rock formation off Yonaguni Island first noted by a diver in 1986, with stepped, angular faces that some read as worked stone and others as natural sandstone fracturing.
heroes.debated: Whether the formation is a shaped structure or the product of natural rock jointing and erosion; most published geological assessments favour a natural origin.

heroes.name: Rujm el-Hiri
heroes.summary: Five concentric rings of loose basalt stone on the Golan plateau, with a burial cairn at the centre, built in the Early Bronze Age. Also known as Gilgal Refaim, the wheel of giants.
heroes.debated: What the rings were for, whether calendar, gathering place or funerary monument, and why the cairn was added centuries after the rings.
heroes.attribution: Academic survey: Paz, 'Rujm el-Hiri: The Monument in the Landscape'
